If indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope. Key words. “If indeed” (eanper, if, provided that). “Hold fast” (kataschōmen, hold firmly, keep a firm grip). “Confidence” (parrēsian, boldness, freedom, openness). “Boasting” (kauchēma, pride, exultation). “Hope”: the certain hope of glory. Membership in God’s house is shown by holding firm.

Where Christians differ: does this conditional mean true believers can be lost? Arminians read the “if” as meaning that a genuine member of God’s house may fall away and cease to be part of it. Verdict: The verse says we are his house if we hold fast; it does not say we will cease to be his house if we do not. Holding fast is the evidence of genuine membership, not the cause of it. Verse 14 makes the logic clearer: we have come to share in Christ (perfect tense, already true), if we hold firm to the end. Perseverance proves that we have truly come to share in him. Those who fall away show they never did (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and God uses it as a means to keep his people persevering (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean our salvation depends on our own strength to hold on. Christ holds us (John 10:28). But we are called to hold fast, and those whom he holds do hold fast.

In a sentence. Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s household, bearing witness to what God would say in the future. But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s household. And we are that household, if we keep our grip on our confidence and on the hope we are proud of.

On a Tuesday. Hold fast today to your confidence in Christ. Speak of your hope to someone, unashamed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–19 — Today, If You Hear His Voice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Holy Spirit says, from Psalm 95: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” as Israel did in the wilderness, testing God for forty years until he swore they would not enter his rest. So take care that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns from the living God. Encourage one another daily, so that no one is hardened by sin’s deceit. We share in Christ if we hold firm to the end. Those who fell in the wilderness were the very people rescued from Egypt, and they could not enter because of unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remedy Is Other People

Because sin deceives, a hardening heart cannot diagnose itself. So the safeguard is outside the individual: exhort one another every day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those who fell in the wilderness were the ones who had come out of Egypt.

Now: They stayed out through unbelief, so belief is the way in, and no one is too far gone to exercise it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was provoked with that generation, and said, ’They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways.’ As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was provoked with that generation, and said, ‘They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways.’ As I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter my rest.’”

Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says. Key words. The quotation is from Psalm 95:7–11, written by David (4:7). Yet the author says the Holy Spirit says it, present tense. Scripture is the Spirit’s word, and it speaks now, to us (10:15; 2 Peter 1:21). This is a strong statement of the inspiration and present authority of Scripture.

Today, if you hear his voice. Key words. “Today” (sēmeron): the key word of the warning, repeated in verses 13 and 15 and in 4:7. Every day God’s word is heard is a “today,” a moment of opportunity and responsibility. It will not last forever.

Do not harden your hearts. Key words. “Harden” (sklērynēte, make stiff, stubborn). The heart becomes hard through repeated refusal to listen (Exodus 8:15). Each refusal makes the next easier.

As in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness. Key words. “Rebellion” (parapikrasmō, provocation, embitterment) translates Meribah; “testing” (peirasmou) translates Massah. Meribah (“quarrelling”) and Massah (“testing”) were where Israel complained for water and doubted God’s presence, soon after leaving Egypt (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:1–13). But the psalm refers to the whole pattern of the forty years.

Where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years. Key words. “Put me to the test” (epeirasan, tried, tested): demanding that God prove himself. They had seen the plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock, the cloud and fire. Yet they doubted. Seeing miracles does not create faith in a hard heart.

Therefore I was provoked with that generation. Key words. “Provoked” (prosōchthisa, angered, disgusted, offended). God’s holy anger at persistent unbelief.

They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways. Key words. “Go astray” (planōntai, wander, err). The problem was the heart. “Not known my ways”: not intellectual ignorance (they saw everything) but a refusal to know God personally and walk in his ways.

As I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter my rest. Key words. “Swore”: God’s solemn oath (Numbers 14:21–23, 28–35). “Rest” (katapausin): originally the rest of the promised land of Canaan (Deuteronomy 12:9). Chapter 4 will show that God’s rest is something greater: the eternal rest of salvation.

What it does not mean. “They shall not enter my rest” does not mean every individual in that generation was eternally lost; Moses and Aaron died in the wilderness, and Caleb and Joshua entered. But it shows the seriousness of persistent unbelief, and it serves as a type of eternal exclusion for those who finally reject God.

In a sentence. So, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not make your hearts stubborn as you did in the rebellion, when you tested me in the wilderness. There your ancestors tried me and tested me, though for forty years they saw what I did. That is why I was angry with that generation; I said, ‘Their hearts are always going astray, and they have not known my ways.’ So I declared on oath in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest.’”

On a Tuesday. Today, as you read God’s word, do not harden your heart. Is there something God has been telling you that you keep putting off? Respond today.
verseByVerse.note: Meribah (“quarreling”) and Massah (“testing”) were where Israel tested God for water.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God.

Take care, brothers. Key words. “Take care” (blepete, watch out, see to it, be on guard). A warning to the whole community. “Brothers”: addressed to professing believers.

Lest there be in any of you. Key words. “Any of you” (en tini hymōn): even one. Each person matters; the church must watch for each member.

An evil, unbelieving heart. Key words. “Evil” (ponēra, wicked). “Unbelieving” (apistias, of unbelief). Unbelief is not merely intellectual doubt; it is a moral evil, a heart that refuses to trust God. At root, unbelief calls God a liar (1 John 5:10).

Leading you to fall away from the living God. Key words. “Fall away” (apostēnai, depart, withdraw, apostatise). “The living God”: for these Jewish readers, turning back from Christ to Judaism would not be returning to God; it would be turning away from the living God himself, who has spoken in his Son (1:2). There is no access to God apart from Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every doubt or struggle is apostasy. Believers struggle with doubt (Mark 9:24; Jude 22). Apostasy is the settled, deliberate turning away from Christ. Nor does it imply that true believers will finally fall away; the warning is one of the means God uses to keep them from doing so.

In a sentence. Be careful, brothers and sisters, that none of you has a wicked, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.

On a Tuesday. Examine your own heart today: is there unbelief growing there? Bring it to God honestly and ask him for faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.

But exhort one another every day. Key words. “Exhort” (parakaleite, encourage, urge, come alongside). Present tense: keep doing it. “One another” (heautous): mutual, every believer to every other. “Every day” (kath’ hekastēn hēmeran): not just on Sundays. Believers need daily encouragement to persevere. The antidote to hardening is fellowship. Isolated Christians are vulnerable.

As long as it is called today. Key words. “Today” from Psalm 95. The day of opportunity will not last forever, both because life is short and because Christ will return. Encourage now.

That none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Key words. “Hardened” (sklērynthē), passive: hardened by sin. “Deceitfulness” (apatē, deception, trickery). Sin deceives: it promises pleasure, freedom and satisfaction, and delivers slavery, emptiness and death. It hardens gradually, without our noticing. We need others to see what we cannot see in ourselves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only pastors should encourage. Every believer has this responsibility. Nor does “exhort” mean nag or criticise; it is warm, honest, loving urging.

In a sentence. Instead, encourage one another every day, as long as it is still called “today,” so that none of you is hardened by sin and its deceptions.

On a Tuesday. Who will you encourage today? Send a message, make a call, or say a word to a fellow believer to help them keep going.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end. As it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end. As it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”

For we have come to share in Christ. Key words. “Have come to share” (metochoi gegonamen, we have become partners, perfect tense: we have become and remain). “Share in Christ” (tou Christou): partners with Christ, sharing in him and his blessings (3:1; 6:4).

If indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end. Key words. “Original confidence” (tēn archēn tēs hypostaseōs, the beginning of our assurance, our first conviction). “Hold firm” (bebaian kataschōmen, keep secure). “To the end” (mechri telous): to the end of life or to Christ’s return. The grammar is important: we have come to share in Christ (a past fact, still true) if we hold firm. Holding firm is the evidence that we have truly come to share in Christ. It does not make us share in him; it shows we already do.

As it is said, Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion. Key words. The psalm is quoted again (v. 7) to drive home the urgency.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is uncertain until death. Assurance is possible and good (6:11; 10:22). But assurance is grounded in Christ and confirmed by perseverance. Those who persevere know they have truly come to share in Christ; those who do not, show they never did.

In a sentence. For we have become partners with Christ, as long as we keep hold of the confidence we had at the start, firmly to the end. As Scripture says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as you did in the rebellion.”

For worship. Thank God that he has made you a sharer in Christ, and pray for grace to hold firm to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient?

For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Key words. Three questions with three answers, drawn from Numbers 14. “Heard”: they heard God’s voice. “Rebelled” (parepikranan, provoked, embittered).

Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? Key words. The shocking answer: the very people who had been redeemed from Egypt, who had experienced God’s great salvation, who had crossed the Red Sea and been led by Moses. Privilege did not protect them. The readers were in a similar position: they had heard the gospel and seen God’s work.

And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Key words. Forty years of patience and provocation.

Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? Key words. “Bodies” (kōla, limbs, corpses). Vivid: their corpses littered the desert (Numbers 14:29, 32). A sobering picture.

And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? Key words. “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin, refused to be persuaded, rebelled). Disobedience and unbelief are two sides of the same coin (v. 19). Unbelief shows itself in disobedience; disobedience flows from unbelief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that everyone who leaves a church is like the wilderness generation, or that every sin brings this judgement. It warns against settled unbelief that refuses to trust God despite all he has done.

In a sentence. Who were they who heard and yet rebelled? Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt? And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would never enter his rest, if not to those who disobeyed?

On a Tuesday. Privilege does not equal faith. Do not rely on your church background or past experiences. Trust Christ today.

verseByVerse.quote: So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.

So we see. Key words. “See” (blepomen): we can observe the lesson clearly from history.

That they were unable to enter. Key words. “Unable” (ouk ēdynēthēsan, could not). They did try to enter Canaan, the day after God’s oath, in their own strength, and were defeated (Numbers 14:39–45). Without faith, entry is impossible.

Because of unbelief. Key words. “Unbelief” (apistian). The root cause of their failure. Not lack of evidence, not lack of opportunity, but lack of faith. They did not believe God would keep his promise and give them the land (Numbers 14:11). Unbelief is the sin behind all sins, the refusal to take God at his word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that earns entry. Faith receives what God gives. But without it, the gift is refused. Nor does it mean that unbelief is beyond God’s mercy if repented of; the warning is given so that we will not harden ourselves.

In a sentence. So we see that it was their unbelief that kept them from entering.

For worship. Ask God to give you a believing heart that takes him at his word, every day, until you enter his rest.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, holy brothers, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,<sup>2</sup>who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house.<sup>3</sup>For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses—as much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.<sup>4</sup>(For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.)<sup>5</sup>Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later,<sup>6</sup>but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.<sup>7</sup>Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice,<sup>8</sup>do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness,<sup>9</sup>where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years.<sup>10</sup>Therefore I was provoked with that generation, and said, ’They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways.’<sup>11</sup>As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest.’”<sup>12</sup>Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God.<sup>13</sup>But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.<sup>14</sup>For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end.<sup>15</sup>As it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”<sup>16</sup>For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses?<sup>17</sup>And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?<sup>18</sup>And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient?<sup>19</sup>So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.

4.title: A Rest That Remains: The Throne of Grace
4.overview:
Chapter 4 develops one of the most original arguments in the New Testament. The rest God promised was not fully given under Joshua; otherwise, why would God say through David, centuries later, “Today, if you hear his voice”? So the rest remains. And it is not a land or a day, but a share in God’s own Sabbath rest: the rest of finished work. To enter it is to stop working to justify ourselves and trust what Christ has finished.

The chapter ends with a sword and an invitation. God’s word lays us bare; nothing is hidden. And then: since we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Remains a Sabbath Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise of entering God’s rest still stands, so let us take care that none of us falls short. The wilderness generation heard good news, but it did not benefit them because they did not receive it with faith. We who believe enter that rest. God’s rest has existed since he rested on the seventh day, and centuries after Joshua God still said “Today”. So a Sabbath rest remains for God’s people: to rest from our works as God did from his. Let us strive to enter it.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Rest That Remains

Psalm 95 still says today centuries after Joshua, so the land was never the rest itself. What remains is a Sabbath rest: ceasing from our own works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The wilderness generation heard good news, and it did not benefit them because it was not united with faith.

Now: Strive to enter that rest. Trusting God is harder work than being busy for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.

Meaning first. Hebrews 4 continues the warning of chapter 3 and explains what God’s “rest” really is. The promise of entering God’s rest still stands, so the readers must take care not to fall short of it; the wilderness generation heard good news too, but it did not help them because they did not believe (vv. 1–2). Those who believe do enter that rest (v. 3). What rest is it? Not merely Canaan: God’s own rest began on the seventh day of creation, when he finished his works (vv. 3–5). Since Psalm 95, written long after Joshua led Israel into Canaan, still speaks of entering God’s rest “today,” Joshua cannot have given the final rest (vv. 6–8). So there remains a Sabbath rest for God’s people: resting from our own works as God rested from his (vv. 9–10). Therefore we must strive to enter it (v. 11). And we cannot hide behind religious appearances, because God’s word is living and active, sharper than any sword, exposing the heart, and everything lies naked before the God to whom we must give account (vv. 12–13). But we are not left alone with that exposure: we have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens, who sympathises with our weakness, having been tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin. So let us hold fast and draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (vv. 14–16).

Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands. Key words. “Promise” (epangelias). “Still stands” (kataleipomenēs, being left behind, remaining open). The offer of God’s rest was not withdrawn when Israel failed; it is still open now.

Let us fear. Key words. “Fear” (phobēthōmen). A healthy, reverent fear of falling short: not terror, but the seriousness of someone who knows what is at stake (Philippians 2:12; 1 Peter 1:17).

Lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. Key words. “Seem” (dokē, appear, be found, be judged). “Failed to reach” (hysterēkenai, fall short, come too late, lag behind). Like a traveller arriving after the gates have closed.

For good news came to us just as to them. Key words. “Good news came” (euēngelismenoi, we have had the gospel preached). The wilderness generation heard good news: the promise of the land. We have heard the greater good news of Christ.

But the message they heard did not benefit them. Key words. “Did not benefit” (ouk ōphelēsen, did not profit). Hearing is not enough.

Because they were not united by faith with those who listened. Key words. “United” (synkekerasmenous, mixed together, blended). The message was not mixed with faith in the hearers. Some manuscripts read it as the message not being combined with faith; others as the hearers not being united in faith with those who truly listened (Joshua and Caleb). Either way: the word must be received with faith to benefit. Food that is not eaten does not nourish.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that adds to the gospel. Faith is the empty hand that receives it. Nor does “let us fear” contradict assurance; it is the fear that drives us to Christ, not away from him.

In a sentence. So, since God’s promise of entering his rest is still open, let us be careful that none of you turns out to have fallen short of it. We have had the good news announced to us just as they did, but the message they heard did them no good, because they did not combine it with faith.

On a Tuesday. Are you hearing God’s word without mixing it with faith? As you read Scripture today, respond: believe it, trust it, act on it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”

For we who have believed enter that rest. Key words. “Have believed” (pisteusantes, aorist: those who came to faith). “Enter” (eiserchometha, present tense: are entering). Believers enter God’s rest now, in part: rest from the burden of earning salvation, peace with God, rest of conscience (Matthew 11:28–29; Romans 5:1). And they will enter it fully in glory. The rest is both present and future.

As he has said, As I swore in my wrath, They shall not enter my rest. Key words. Psalm 95:11 again. The negative proves the positive: unbelievers are excluded, so believers enter.

Although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. Key words. “Finished” (genēthentōn, completed). God’s rest is not something new. It has existed since creation was finished. It is God’s own rest, and he invites his people to share it.

For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: And God rested on the seventh day from all his works. Key words. From Genesis 2:2. God “rested” (katepausen, ceased) not because he was tired (Isaiah 40:28), but because his work of creation was complete. Notably, the seventh day in Genesis has no “evening and morning” formula; God’s rest has no end. It is an ongoing state of completed satisfaction.

And again in this passage he said, They shall not enter my rest. Key words. Putting Genesis 2:2 and Psalm 95:11 together: the rest Israel failed to enter was God’s own Sabbath rest, of which Canaan was only a picture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God stopped all activity on the seventh day; he continues to uphold all things (1:3; John 5:17). He ceased from the work of creating.

In a sentence. Now we who have believed are entering that rest, just as God said, “So I declared on oath in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest.’” And yet his works have been finished since the creation of the world. For somewhere he has spoken about the seventh day in these words: “On the seventh day God rested from all his works.” And again, in the passage above, he says, “They shall never enter my rest.”

For worship. Thank God that through faith in Christ you have begun to enter his rest: peace with God, and freedom from striving to earn his favour.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.

Since therefore it remains for some to enter it. Key words. “Remains” (apoleipetai, is left over, still open). God’s purpose is that some will enter his rest. The failure of one generation did not cancel his plan.

And those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience. Key words. The wilderness generation.

Again he appoints a certain day, Today. Key words. “Appoints” (horizei, sets, defines, marks out). God fixed a new day of opportunity.

Saying through David so long afterward. Key words. Psalm 95 is attributed to David in the Greek translation. David lived about four hundred years after Moses and Joshua. If the promise of rest had been fully realised in Canaan, why would David still be offering it, centuries later?

For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on. Key words. Joshua led Israel into Canaan, and the land had rest from war for a time (Joshua 21:44; 23:1). But that was not God’s final rest. In Greek, “Joshua” and “Jesus” are the same name (Iēsous). The first Joshua brought Israel into an earthly land; the greater Joshua, Jesus, brings his people into God’s eternal rest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Joshua failed or that Canaan was not a real gift. It was real, but it was a shadow of something greater, as the whole Old Testament is.

In a sentence. So it is still true that some are to enter that rest, and since those who first had the good news preached to them did not enter because they disobeyed, God again set a particular day, calling it “Today.” He spoke of it through David a long time later, in the words already quoted: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.

For worship. Thank Jesus, the greater Joshua, who leads his people not into a piece of land but into God’s own eternal rest.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.

So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. Key words. “Sabbath rest” (sabbatismos, a Sabbath-keeping, a Sabbath celebration). A rare word, perhaps coined by the author. Not merely “rest” (katapausis) but a festive Sabbath rest, sharing in God’s own celebration of his finished work. “Remains” (apoleipetai): it is still waiting, still to come in its fullness. “People of God”: all who believe.

For whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his. Key words. “Rested from his works” (katepausen apo tōn ergōn autou). Entering God’s rest means ceasing from our own works: ceasing from trying to earn salvation by our efforts, and resting in Christ’s finished work (Romans 4:5). It may also refer to the final rest after the labours of this life (Revelation 14:13). Both are true: now we rest from works as a way of salvation; then we will rest from all toil and suffering.

Where Christians differ: is the weekly Sabbath still binding on Christians? Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that the seventh-day Sabbath is still binding. Many in the Reformed and Puritan tradition hold that the Sabbath commandment continues, transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, with strict rest required. Others see the Sabbath as wholly fulfilled in Christ, with no special day required. Verdict: The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28–12:8; Colossians 2:16–17). Christians are not bound to the Old Testament Sabbath regulations. Yet the pattern of one day in seven is a creation gift, and the early church gathered on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, to celebrate Christ’s resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). Keeping the Lord’s Day for worship, rest and fellowship is a great privilege and wise practice, not a legal burden or a means of earning favour. Those who keep a stricter Sabbath should be respected (Romans 14:5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be idle or stop doing good works. Resting from works as a means of salvation frees us for good works as fruit of salvation (Ephesians 2:8–10). Nor does it mean the final rest has fully arrived; it remains.

In a sentence. So a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God’s people; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their own work, just as God did from his.

For worship. Use the Lord’s Day this week as a gift: rest from your labours, worship the risen Christ, and taste the Sabbath rest that awaits you.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.

Let us therefore strive to enter that rest. Key words. “Strive” (spoudasōmen, make every effort, be diligent, hurry). A paradox: strive to enter rest. We do not strive to earn salvation; we strive to keep believing, to resist hardening, to hold fast (3:6, 14; 2 Peter 1:10). The effort is the effort of faith, which keeps trusting and obeying.

So that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience. Key words. “Fall” (pesē), echoing the bodies that “fell” in the wilderness (3:17). “Same sort” (tō autō hypodeigmati, the same example, pattern). The wilderness generation is a warning example (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is by works. The rest we strive to enter is the rest from works. The striving is to keep trusting Christ and not drift back to self-reliance or unbelief.

In a sentence. So let us make every effort to enter that rest, so that none of us falls by following their example of disobedience.

On a Tuesday. What could cause you to drift from trusting Christ? Strive against it today: by prayer, by Scripture, by staying close to God’s people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Laid Bare, and Invited In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer warns that God’s word is alive and at work, cutting more sharply than any blade, reaching to the deepest parts of a person and exposing the real thoughts and motives of the heart. No creature can hide from God; everything lies open before the one to whom we must give account. But there is an invitation alongside the warning. We have a great high priest who has passed into heaven, Jesus, God’s Son, so we should keep holding to our confession. He is able to feel for our weaknesses, because he was tested in every way as we are, yet without sin. So we can come confidently to God’s throne of grace, to receive mercy and find grace to help us when we need it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Exposure Comes First

The word lays us bare, and only then does the writer say, “since then we have a great high priest”. The one who sees through us is the one who sympathises with us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Drawing near was once the privilege of priests alone.

Now: Come to the throne of grace with confidence — mercy for what lies behind, grace for what lies ahead, help that arrives when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

For the word of God. Key words. “For” explains why we must strive (v. 11): God’s word sees through every pretence. “The word of God” (ho logos tou theou): God’s spoken and written word, here especially the warnings of Psalm 95 just quoted, and all Scripture.

Is living and active. Key words. “Living” (zōn, alive), because it comes from the living God (3:12). “Active” (energēs, effective, powerful, at work). Scripture is not a dead letter. It does things: it convicts, converts, comforts, sanctifies (Isaiah 55:10–11; Jeremiah 23:29; 1 Thessalonians 2:13).

Sharper than any two-edged sword. Key words. “Two-edged” (distomon, two-mouthed). The Roman short sword (machaira), sharp on both sides, used for close combat and surgical precision (Ephesians 6:17; Revelation 1:16).

Piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow. Key words. “Piercing” (diiknoumenos, penetrating right through). “Soul” (psychēs) and “spirit” (pneumatos), “joints” (harmōn) and “marrow” (myelōn). A vivid picture of the word penetrating to the deepest, most hidden parts of a person. The point is not anatomical precision but total penetration: nothing is beyond its reach.

And discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Key words. “Discerning” (kritikos, able to judge; our word “critical”). “Thoughts” (enthymēseōn, reflections, ideas). “Intentions” (ennoiōn, purposes, motives). The word judges not just our actions but our motives. We do not judge Scripture; it judges us.

Where Christians differ: are soul and spirit two different parts of a person? Some teach a threefold view of human nature (body, soul and spirit as three distinct parts), using this verse and 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Verdict: Scripture generally uses soul and spirit interchangeably for the immaterial part of a person (Luke 1:46–47; John 12:27 and 13:21; Matthew 10:28). The body-and-soul view (dichotomy) fits the overall biblical teaching best. This verse does not teach that soul and spirit are separate components; like joints and marrow, it pictures the word cutting to the very core of a person.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture works like magic apart from the Spirit. The Spirit uses the word. Nor does it mean the “word of God” here refers primarily to Jesus as the Word (John 1:1), though he is the one who speaks it.

In a sentence. For God’s word is alive and powerful, sharper than any double-edged sword. It cuts right through, to where soul and spirit, joints and marrow meet, and it judges the thoughts and motives of the heart.

On a Tuesday. Read Scripture today and let it read you. Ask: what thoughts and motives is God exposing in my heart?

verseByVerse.quote: And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.

And no creature is hidden from his sight. Key words. “Creature” (ktisis, created thing). “Hidden” (aphanēs, invisible, concealed). The subject shifts from the word to God himself. Nothing in all creation escapes his knowledge (Psalm 139:1–16; Proverbs 15:3; Jeremiah 23:24).

But all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him. Key words. “Naked” (gymna, bare, uncovered). “Exposed” (tetrachēlismena, laid bare, literally with the neck bent back). The word was used of a wrestler gripping his opponent by the throat to throw him, or of a sacrificial animal with its neck bent back to expose the throat for the knife, or of a criminal forced to look up at the judge. Every face lifted, nothing hidden.

To whom we must give account. Key words. Literally “with whom is our word” (pros hon hēmin ho logos): a play on “word” in verse 12. God’s word judges us, and we must give our word, our account, to him. Every person will stand before God (Romans 14:12; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God watches only to condemn. For those in Christ, being fully known is the beginning of being fully loved and healed. The next verses turn immediately to the high priest who sympathises.

In a sentence. Nothing in all creation is hidden from God. Everything is uncovered and laid bare before the eyes of the one to whom we must give our account.

For worship. Confess before God what you have been hiding. He already sees it, and in Christ, he will forgive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.

Since then we have a great high priest. Key words. “Great high priest” (archierea megan). Aaron was the high priest; Jesus is the great high priest. The main theme of chapters 4–10 begins here.

Who has passed through the heavens. Key words. “Passed through” (dielēlythota, gone through, perfect tense). The Old Testament high priest passed through the courts and the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year (Leviticus 16). Jesus has passed through the heavens into the very presence of God (9:24), at his ascension. The tabernacle was a copy; Christ entered the reality.

Jesus, the Son of God. Key words. “Jesus”: his human name, the man who suffered. “Son of God”: his divine identity. Both together qualify him to be our high priest: truly human to represent us, truly divine to make his sacrifice infinitely effective.

Let us hold fast our confession. Key words. “Hold fast” (kratōmen, grip firmly, take hold strongly). “Confession” (homologias), as in 3:1.

For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. Key words. “Sympathize” (sympathēsai, suffer with, feel together with; our word “sympathy”). “Weaknesses” (astheneiais, frailties, infirmities, limitations). The double negative (“not unable”) emphasises: he can and does sympathise. He is not a distant, unfeeling figure.

But one who in every respect has been tempted as we are. Key words. “In every respect” (kata panta, in all things). “Tempted” (pepeirasmenon, tested, tried, perfect tense: experienced and still knows it). Jesus faced every kind of temptation humans face: to doubt God, to take shortcuts, to avoid suffering, to seek glory, to give up. Not every specific temptation in every circumstance, but every type, at full force.

Yet without sin. Key words. “Without sin” (chōris hamartias). He never sinned, in thought, word or deed (7:26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). Because he never yielded, he felt the full weight of temptation, as a person who never gives in feels the full pressure of the wind.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some argue that if he could not have sinned, his temptations were not real. Verdict: The Son of God could not sin, because he is God, and God cannot sin (James 1:13). Yet his temptations were real, because his human nature genuinely felt their pull, and he resisted by faith, prayer and the Spirit’s power as a true man. A bridge that cannot collapse is still truly tested by the weight of the trucks that cross it. His impeccability does not lessen his sympathy; it makes his help sure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus’ temptations were identical to ours in every detail, or that he experienced the temptations that arise from already having sinned. It means he knows temptation from the inside, and can help.

In a sentence. So, since we have a great high priest who has gone through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us keep a firm grip on the faith we confess. For our high priest is not one who cannot feel for us in our weaknesses; he has been tested in every way, just as we are, yet he never sinned.

For worship. Bring your weakness to Jesus today. He feels with you, and he has overcome.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

Let us then with confidence draw near. Key words. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha, approach, come toward), present tense: keep coming. The language of priests approaching God in worship (Leviticus 9:7; 21:17). In the old covenant, only the high priest could approach God’s presence, once a year, with blood. Now every believer can come, at any time. “Confidence” (parrēsias, boldness, freedom of speech, openness). Not arrogance, but freedom to come without fear, because of our high priest (10:19–22).

To the throne of grace. Key words. “Throne”: God’s royal seat, the place of his authority. For sinners, God’s throne would be a throne of judgement. But because of our high priest, it is a throne of grace (tō thronō tēs charitos), where grace is dispensed. The mercy seat on the ark was God’s throne in the Most Holy Place (Exodus 25:22).

That we may receive mercy. Key words. “Receive mercy” (labōmen eleos). Mercy for our failures and sins: pity, forgiveness.

And find grace to help in time of need. Key words. “Grace to help” (charin eis eukairon boētheian, grace for timely help). “In time of need” (eukairon, at the right moment, well-timed). Grace that arrives exactly when needed. “Help” (boētheian, running to aid at a cry), the same word as 2:18. Mercy deals with our past; grace helps us now and for what is coming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should come casually or irreverently. We come with confidence, but to a throne. Nor does it mean we need saints, priests or Mary to approach for us; Christ is our only and sufficient high priest (1 Timothy 2:5).

In a sentence. So let us come boldly to the throne where grace is given, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us at the moment we need it.

For worship. Come to God in prayer right now, boldly, through Jesus. Ask for mercy for what you have done and grace for what you face.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it.<sup>2</sup>For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.<sup>3</sup>For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world.<sup>4</sup>For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.”<sup>5</sup>And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”<sup>6</sup>Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly 5.title: The Qualifications of the Perfect Priest
5.overview:
Chapter 5 opens the letter’s central theme: Jesus as a priest after the order of Melchizedek. The writer first sets out what every true high priest must be: chosen from among men, acting for them before God, able to deal gently with the weak, and called by God rather than self-appointed. Jesus meets every qualification, without the fatal flaw of needing to offer for his own sins.

Psalm 110:4, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek”, opens an argument that runs to chapter 7. Then comes a tender picture of Jesus praying “with loud cries and tears”, heard because of his reverence, learning obedience through suffering. And then, abruptly, a rebuke: the readers have become dull of hearing, still on milk when they should be eating solid food.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer explains what a high priest is. He is taken from among human beings and appointed to act for them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins. Because he shares their weakness, he can be gentle with the ignorant and the straying, and he must offer sacrifices for his own sins too. No one can take the office for himself; God must call him, as he called Aaron. Christ likewise did not appoint himself, but was appointed by the God who called him his Son and declared him a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek. In his earthly life Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and was heard because of his reverent submission. Son though he was, he learned obedience through suffering, and once made complete he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him, named by God a high priest like Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.theology:
Appointed, Not Self-Chosen

A high priest must share the weakness of those he represents and be called by God. Christ meets both, without the flaw of needing to offer for his own sins, and is named a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the days of his flesh he prayed with loud cries and tears, and was heard.

Now: An answer that does not come in the form we asked for is not proof that we were unheard.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness. Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness. Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.

Meaning first. Hebrews 5 explains what qualifies someone to be a high priest and shows that Jesus meets every qualification, and more. A high priest must be taken from among human beings to represent them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices for sins; he must be able to deal gently with the ignorant and straying, since he shares their weakness; and he must be called by God, as Aaron was, rather than appointing himself (vv. 1–4). Christ too did not appoint himself: God appointed him, the one he called his Son, and declared him a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek (vv. 5–6). Christ shared human weakness: in the days of his earthly life he prayed with loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission; though he was the Son, he learned obedience through suffering, and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him (vv. 7–10). Then the author pauses: there is much more to say about Melchizedek, but it is hard to explain because the readers have become sluggish in hearing. They ought to be teachers by now, but they need milk again, the basics, rather than solid food, which belongs to the mature who have trained their discernment by practice (vv. 11–14).

For every high priest chosen from among men. Key words. “High priest” (archiereus): in Israel, the descendant of Aaron who led the priesthood and entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. “Chosen from among men” (ex anthrōpōn lambanomenos, taken from humans). The first qualification: he must be human, one of the people he represents. This is why the Son had to become man (2:14–17).

Is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God. Key words. “On behalf of men” (hyper anthrōpōn, for people). “In relation to God” (ta pros ton theon, the things concerning God), as in 2:17. A priest is a go-between who represents people to God, as a prophet represents God to people.

To offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. Key words. “Gifts” (dōra, offerings, perhaps grain offerings) and “sacrifices” (thysias, animal sacrifices). The central work of a priest: dealing with sin through offering (8:3).

He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward. Key words. “Deal gently” (metriopathein, moderate one’s feelings, be neither too harsh nor too lenient, show measured sympathy). A rare word: he does not explode in anger at sinners, nor excuse sin. “Ignorant” (agnoousin, those who sin in ignorance) and “wayward” (planōmenois, those who wander, go astray). The Old Testament sacrifices covered sins of ignorance and weakness, not defiant, high-handed sins (Numbers 15:27–31).

Since he himself is beset with weakness. Key words. “Beset” (perikeitai, surrounded by, clothed with, like a garment or a chain). He knows weakness from the inside.

Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people. Key words. On the Day of Atonement, Aaron first offered a bull for his own sins and his household, then a goat for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 11, 15). Here Jesus is different: he shares our weakness but not our sin (4:15; 7:27). He needs no sacrifice for himself.

Where Christians differ: are Christian ministers priests? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches call their clergy priests, who offer the sacrifice of the Mass on behalf of the people. Verdict: The New Testament never calls Christian ministers priests (hiereis) in this sense. Jesus is the one and only high priest of the new covenant, whose sacrifice was offered once for all (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–14). There is no further sacrifice for sin to offer. All believers together are a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices of praise and good works (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Hebrews 13:15–16). Ministers are elders and shepherds, not sacrificing priests. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance and spiritual feeding on Christ, not a re-offering of him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus was a sinner like Aaron. He shares our weakness, not our sin.

In a sentence. Every high priest is selected from among people and appointed to represent them before God, to present gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is surrounded by weakness. That is why he has to offer sacrifices for his own sins as well as for the people’s.

For worship. Thank God that you have a perfect high priest who never needs to offer for himself, and who deals gently with you in your weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.

And no one takes this honor for himself. Key words. “Honor” (timēn, dignity, office). The high priesthood was an honour, but not one to grab. Those who seized priestly functions for themselves were judged: Korah (Numbers 16), King Saul (1 Samuel 13:8–14), King Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

But only when called by God, just as Aaron was. Key words. “Called” (kaloumenos). God chose Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1; Numbers 17–18). The second qualification of a priest: divine appointment.

Setting and background. By the first century, the high priesthood had become political. Herod and the Romans appointed and removed high priests at will, often selling the office. The readers would know how far the office had fallen from God’s design. The author goes back to the ideal: God’s calling.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all ministry today requires a special supernatural call experience. Ministers today are called through the church’s recognition of their gifts and character (1 Timothy 3:1–7). But no one should take spiritual office simply out of ambition.

In a sentence. No one takes this honour on himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was.

On a Tuesday. Are you seeking honour for yourself? Serve where God has placed you, and let him do the exalting (1 Peter 5:6).

verseByVerse.quote: So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”; as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”; as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”

So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest. Key words. “Exalt himself” (edoxasen heauton, glorify himself). Jesus did not seize the priesthood. He came to do the Father’s will (John 8:54; 10:18).

But was appointed by him who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Key words. Psalm 2:7, already quoted in 1:5. The Father who declared him Son also appointed him priest. His sonship and priesthood go together.

As he says also in another place, You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek. Key words. Psalm 110:4, the key text for chapters 5–7. Psalm 110:1 (the Messiah seated at God’s right hand) was quoted in 1:13. Now verse 4 of the same psalm: the Messiah-King is also a priest. “Forever” (eis ton aiōna): unlike Aaron’s priests, who died. “Order of Melchizedek” (kata tēn taxin Melchisedek, the rank, kind, type of Melchizedek). Melchizedek was a priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20). He was not descended from Levi or Aaron; his priesthood was of a different and earlier kind. Chapter 7 will explain fully.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ became Son at his appointment as priest. He is the eternal Son (1:2–3). His eternal sonship qualifies him to be appointed eternal priest.

In a sentence. In the same way, Christ did not give himself the glory of becoming high priest. God said to him, “You are my Son; today I have become your Father.” And in another place he says, “You are a priest for ever, in the order of Melchizedek.”

For worship. Praise God the Father for appointing his Son to be your eternal priest, and praise the Son who accepted that calling for you.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.

In the days of his flesh. Key words. “Flesh” (sarkos): his earthly life in human weakness, before his resurrection and glorification.

Jesus offered up prayers and supplications. Key words. “Offered up” (prosenenkas), the priestly word for offering sacrifices (v. 1). His prayers were part of his priestly offering. “Supplications” (hiketērias, earnest pleas, the word for a suppliant holding an olive branch).

With loud cries and tears. Key words. “Loud cries” (kraugēs ischyras, strong crying). “Tears” (dakryōn). Most likely a reference to Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane, where he was “very sorrowful, even to death,” sweat like drops of blood, and prayed three times for the cup to pass (Matthew 26:36–46; Luke 22:39–46). Perhaps also the cries from the cross (Mark 15:34, 37). His suffering was real and his human anguish deep.

To him who was able to save him from death. Key words. The Father, who could have rescued him from dying. Or “out of death” (ek thanatou): bring him through death and out of it, in resurrection.

And he was heard because of his reverence. Key words. “Heard” (eisakoustheis): his prayer was answered. “Reverence” (eulabeias, godly fear, reverent submission). How was he heard, if he still died? Jesus prayed above all, “not my will, but yours” (Luke 22:42). That prayer was answered: the Father’s will was done, and Jesus was strengthened (Luke 22:43), and then saved out of death by resurrection. He was heard, not by escaping death, but by triumphing over it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus lacked faith or tried to escape his mission. His prayer expressed true human dread of the cup of God’s wrath, combined with perfect submission. Nor does it mean his tears were weakness; they were the measure of what he bore for us.

In a sentence. During his life on earth, Jesus offered prayers and pleas, with loud crying and tears, to the one who could rescue him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission.

For worship. When you pray in anguish, remember Jesus in Gethsemane. Pray as he did: honestly, and “not my will, but yours.”
verseByVerse.note: Most likely a reference to Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

Although he was a son. Key words. “Son” (huios). Being the Son of God, one might think he would be exempt from suffering. Yet he suffered.

He learned obedience through what he suffered. Key words. A Greek wordplay: “he learned” (emathen) “from what he suffered” (epathen). He did not learn to obey as one moving from disobedience to obedience; he was never disobedient. He learned what obedience costs by experiencing it in suffering. His obedience was tested, proved and completed as he obeyed to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). Knowledge gained by experience is different from knowledge in principle.

And being made perfect. Key words. “Made perfect” (teleiōtheis, completed, fully qualified), as in 2:10. Through suffering and obedience, he was fully equipped as Saviour and High Priest.

He became the source of eternal salvation. Key words. “Source” (aitios, cause, author). “Eternal salvation” (sōtērias aiōniou): salvation that lasts forever, unlike the temporary effects of the old sacrifices (9:12).

To all who obey him. Key words. “Obey” (hypakouousin, listen to, respond to, obey). As he obeyed the Father, his people obey him. Obedience here is the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5; 16:26), the response of those who trust and follow Christ, in contrast with the disobedience of the wilderness generation (3:18; 4:6, 11).

Being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek. Key words. “Designated” (prosagoreutheis, addressed, named, hailed). God formally proclaimed him high priest. The words of Psalm 110:4 are repeated as the theme to be developed.

What it does not mean. “All who obey him” does not mean salvation is earned by obedience. The obedience in view is trusting, submitting to and following Christ, which is the fruit and expression of faith. Those who truly believe will obey; those who refuse to obey show they do not believe (John 3:36, where disbelief and disobedience are paralleled). Nor does “learned obedience” imply Jesus was ever disobedient.

In a sentence. Son though he was, he learned what obedience means through his suffering. And once he had been made fully qualified, he became the cause of eternal salvation for everyone who obeys him, and God named him high priest in the order of Melchizedek.

On a Tuesday. Is there an area where obedience to Christ will cost you this week? Follow him through it, as he learned obedience through suffering for you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer wants to say more about Melchizedek, but it is hard to explain because his readers have grown sluggish in listening. By this time they ought to be teaching others, yet they need someone to teach them the first principles all over again. Like infants, they need milk rather than solid food. Someone still on milk is not practised in the teaching about righteousness, whereas solid food is for the mature, whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant use to tell good from evil.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Maturity Actually Is

Maturity is not a store of information but a trained faculty — discernment exercised by constant practice until it can tell good from evil.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers had become dull of hearing; they had not always been so.

Now: When Scripture seems dry, ask whether the dullness is in the passage or in the hearer.

verseByVerse.quote: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.

About this we have much to say. Key words. “About this”: about Melchizedek and Christ’s priesthood, or about Christ himself as priest. There is a great deal more.

And it is hard to explain. Key words. “Hard to explain” (dysermēneutos, difficult to interpret, hard to put into words). Not because the truth is unclear, but because of the hearers’ condition.

Since you have become dull of hearing. Key words. “Become” (gegonate, perfect tense: you have become and are now). They were not always like this; they had grown sluggish. “Dull” (nōthroi, sluggish, lazy, slow, numb). The same word in 6:12 (“sluggish”). “Of hearing” (tais akoais, in your ears). Their spiritual hearing had grown lazy. This is a moral and spiritual problem, not intellectual: they had stopped listening attentively, perhaps because truth demanded change or suffering.

What it does not mean. It does not mean deep truths are only for the intellectually gifted. The problem is not ability but attentiveness and spiritual appetite.

In a sentence. We have a great deal to say on this subject, and it is difficult to explain, because you have become slow to listen.

On a Tuesday. Have you become sluggish in hearing God’s word? Ask God to sharpen your spiritual hearing, and come to church this Sunday ready to listen.

verseByVerse.quote: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.

For though by this time you ought to be teachers. Key words. “By this time” (dia ton chronon, because of the time): they had been believers for years. “Ought to be teachers” (opheilontes einai didaskaloi): not that all should hold a teaching office (James 3:1), but that they should be mature enough to explain the faith to others.

You need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. Key words. “Again” (palin): they had gone backwards. “Basic principles” (ta stoicheia tēs archēs, the ABCs, elementary letters of the beginning). “Oracles of God” (tōn logiōn tou theou, God’s utterances, revelation): the basic truths of Scripture.

You need milk, not solid food. Key words. “Milk” (galaktos): elementary teaching, suitable for new converts (1 Corinthians 3:1–2; 1 Peter 2:2). “Solid food” (stereas trophēs, firm nourishment): deeper teaching, such as Christ’s Melchizedek priesthood.

For everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness. Key words. “Unskilled” (apeiros, inexperienced, unacquainted). “Word of righteousness” (logou dikaiosynēs): either the teaching about righteousness (the gospel of how God makes sinners righteous), or right teaching in general, or the skill of using God’s word to discern right from wrong. Probably the last: they lack experience in applying God’s word to life.

Since he is a child. Key words. “Child” (nēpios, infant, baby). Spiritual infancy is natural at the start; it is a problem when it lasts too long.

What it does not mean. It does not mean milk is bad or unnecessary. The basics are always foundational (6:1). The problem is staying at that level. Nor does it mean only a few can reach maturity; all believers should grow.

In a sentence. By now you ought to be teaching others, but you need someone to teach you the elementary truths of God’s word all over again. You need milk instead of solid food! Anyone who lives on milk is still a baby and has no experience in handling the message about what is right.

On a Tuesday. What is one step you can take this month to move from milk to solid food: a book, a course, a deeper study of a Bible book?

verseByVerse.quote: But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.

But solid food is for the mature. Key words. “Mature” (teleiōn, complete, grown-up, adult), related to “made perfect” (v. 9). Christian maturity is the goal (6:1; Ephesians 4:13; Colossians 1:28).

For those who have their powers of discernment trained. Key words. “Powers of discernment” (aisthētēria, senses, faculties of perception). Spiritual senses, like a trained palate that can taste the difference between good and bad food. “Trained” (gegymnasmena, exercised, as in a gymnasium), perfect tense: trained and in condition.

By constant practice. Key words. “Constant practice” (dia tēn hexin, by habit, through use, repeated exercise). Maturity does not come by merely hearing more information. It comes through repeatedly applying God’s word in real life, making real choices, until discernment becomes second nature.

To distinguish good from evil. Key words. “Distinguish” (diakrisin, discernment, judgement, discrimination). Not only moral good and evil, but true and false teaching. The readers, tempted back to Judaism, needed to discern that the old covenant, though good, had been surpassed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean mature believers no longer need basic truths. The mature are those who apply the basics more deeply and widely. Nor does maturity come automatically with age or years in church.

In a sentence. But solid food is for grown-ups, whose senses have been trained by constant use to tell good from evil.

On a Tuesday. Train your discernment this week: when you face a decision, stop and ask, “What does God’s word say about this?” and act on it.
