6.title: Press On to Maturity: The Anchor of the Soul
6.overview:
Chapter 6 holds both the most debated and the most encouraging passages in the letter. It begins with a call to maturity: build on the foundations, do not keep relaying them. Then comes the severest warning (vv. 4–8): those who have seen the full light of the gospel and then deliberately turn away cannot be restored to repentance. Its pastoral aim is to shock the drifting into seeing what is at stake.

At once the writer turns: “in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things” (v. 9). He grounds his confidence in God’s faithfulness, who will not forget their love. And the chapter ends with hope as an anchor for the soul, lodged behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner. Everything is secure because the Priest is already inside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Hardest Warning, and the Confidence After It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So the writer urges them to leave the basic teaching about Christ behind and press on to maturity, without laying again the foundation they already have: turning from dead works and trusting God, teaching about ritual washings and the laying on of hands, the resurrection and eternal judgement. Then comes the letter’s sternest warning. Those who have been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift and the goodness of God’s word, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and who then fall away, cannot be brought back to repentance, because they are crucifying the Son of God again and holding him up to contempt. Like land that drinks the rain and produces only thorns, they face a curse. But the writer is confident of better things for his readers, things that belong to salvation. God will not forget their love and service to his people. He wants each of them to show the same eagerness to the end, not becoming lazy, but imitating those who inherit the promises through faith and patience.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Passage Set Out Honestly

Sincere Christians read verses 4–6 differently. The list describes what was received and seen, not what saves; and five verses later the writer calls his readers beloved and speaks of things that belong to salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two fields drink the same rain; the crop shows the soil.

Now: The warning is not addressed to the anxious. God is not unjust so as to overlook love shown in serving the saints.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.

Meaning first. Hebrews 6 holds together the most solemn warning and the strongest assurance in the letter. It begins with a call to move on from the foundational teachings, which the readers already know, to maturity (vv. 1–3). Then comes the third and most sobering warning (vv. 4–8): it is impossible to bring back to repentance those who have experienced the blessings of the gospel community, been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Spirit’s work, and tasted God’s good word and the powers of the coming age, and then have fallen away, because they are crucifying the Son of God again and publicly disgracing him; they are like land that receives rain but produces only thorns, and is burned. But the author immediately says he is confident of better things in the readers’ case, things that accompany salvation, because God will not forget their love shown in serving the saints; he wants them to show the same diligence to the end, imitating those who inherit the promises through faith and patience (vv. 9–12). The chapter ends with assurance (vv. 13–20): God made a promise to Abraham and confirmed it with an oath, swearing by himself; by these two unchangeable things, in which God cannot lie, we who have fled to him have strong encouragement to hold onto our hope, which is a sure and steady anchor for the soul, fixed in the inner sanctuary where Jesus has gone ahead of us as our forerunner and eternal high priest.

Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ. Key words. “Leave” (aphentes, let go of, move on from). Not abandon, but stop going over the basics again and again, as a builder moves from the foundation to the walls. “Elementary doctrine of Christ” (ton tēs archēs tou Christou logon, the word of the beginning of Christ): the first lessons about Christ.

And go on to maturity. Key words. “Go on” (pherōmetha, be carried along, let us be borne forward), passive: carried by God. “Maturity” (teleiotēta, completeness, adulthood), as in 5:14.

Not laying again a foundation. Key words. “Foundation” (themelion). Six foundational teachings, perhaps in three pairs. Many of them had parallels in Judaism, which may be why the readers were tempted to stay with them rather than move on to the distinctive truth of Christ’s priesthood.

Of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God. Key words. The first pair: conversion. “Repentance” (metanoias, change of mind and direction). “Dead works” (nekrōn ergōn): works that lead to death or that come from spiritual death, sinful deeds and perhaps also religious works done to earn salvation (9:14). “Faith toward God”: trusting God.

And of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands. Key words. The second pair: initiation. “Washings” (baptismōn, plural, washings or baptisms): probably instruction about the difference between Christian baptism and Jewish ritual washings and John’s baptism (9:10; Mark 7:4; Acts 19:1–5). “Laying on of hands”: associated with commissioning, blessing, healing and the giving of the Spirit (Acts 8:17; 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14).

The resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. Key words. The third pair: the last things. The bodily resurrection of all people (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15) and God’s final, everlasting judgement (9:27; Matthew 25:46).

And this we will do if God permits. Key words. “If God permits” (eanper epitrepē ho theos). Spiritual progress depends on God. This also prepares for the warning: there is a condition in which God does not permit progress (vv. 4–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the foundations are unimportant or can be forgotten. Every building rests on its foundation. It means believers should build on it, not keep relaying it.

In a sentence. So let us move beyond the elementary teaching about Christ and be carried forward to maturity, without laying the foundation all over again: turning away from deeds that lead to death, faith in God, teaching about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgement. And God permitting, we will move on.

On a Tuesday. Can you explain these six foundations to someone else? If not, learn them. If so, build on them: go deeper into Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,

For it is impossible. Key words. “Impossible” (adynaton), the first word in the Greek sentence, for emphasis. The same word is used of God’s inability to lie (v. 18), of the blood of bulls removing sin (10:4), and of pleasing God without faith (11:6). It is strong: not difficult, but impossible. The main verb, “to restore again to repentance,” comes in verse 6.

In the case of those who have once been enlightened. Key words. “Once” (hapax, once for all). “Enlightened” (phōtisthentas, given light, illuminated). They heard and understood the gospel; the light of truth shone on them (10:32). Some early writers used “enlightened” for baptism.

Who have tasted the heavenly gift. Key words. “Tasted” (geusamenous, experienced). “Heavenly gift” (tēs dōreas tēs epouraniou): the blessings of salvation from heaven, perhaps Christ himself, forgiveness, or the Spirit. They had sampled these blessings within the church community.

And have shared in the Holy Spirit. Key words. “Shared” (metochous genēthentas, became partakers, partners), as in 3:1, 14. They had participated in the Spirit’s work in the community: his convicting power, gifts and blessings, as Judas shared in the apostles’ ministry (Matthew 10:1–8).

And have tasted the goodness of the word of God. Key words. “Goodness” (kalon, beauty, excellence). They had experienced the sweetness of God’s word, its comfort and power, perhaps with joy, like the seed on rocky ground (Matthew 13:20–21).

And the powers of the age to come. Key words. “Powers” (dynameis, miracles, mighty works), as in 2:4. They had witnessed, perhaps even experienced, the miracles that were the foretaste of the coming age.

Where Christians differ: are these true believers? This is one of the most debated passages in Scripture. Four main views: (1) these are genuine believers who lose their salvation (Arminian view); (2) these are genuine believers, but the warning is hypothetical, describing what would happen if they could fall away, which they cannot; (3) these are genuine believers who lose rewards, not salvation; (4) these are people who have experienced the blessings of the gospel community without being truly regenerated, and whose falling away shows they were never truly saved. Verdict: The fourth view best fits the passage and the whole of Scripture. Every phrase in verses 4–5 describes real experiences that can be had without regeneration: being enlightened (understanding the gospel), tasting (experiencing without fully receiving), sharing in the Spirit’s work (as Judas and Balaam did), tasting the word with joy (like the rocky soil). Notably, the passage does not use words like “justified,” “born again,” “saved” or “sanctified” of these people. In verse 9 the author distinguishes them from those who have “things that belong to salvation.” And the land illustration (vv. 7–8) shows the difference: the same rain falls on two kinds of ground, but the fruit reveals the nature of the soil. Scripture elsewhere teaches that those whom God saves he keeps (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:29–30; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real: such people exist, and God uses this warning to stir true believers to persevere.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a believer who struggles, doubts or falls into sin is beyond hope. Peter denied Christ and was restored. The issue is a final, deliberate, public repudiation of Christ.

In a sentence. It is impossible for those who have once had the light shine on them, who have tasted the gift from heaven, who have taken part in the Holy Spirit’s work, who have tasted how good God’s word is and the powers of the coming age,

For worship. Thank God for every blessing you have tasted in his church. But don’t rest on experiences; rest on Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.

And then have fallen away. Key words. “Fallen away” (parapesontas, fallen aside, apostatised). Not a single sin, but a decisive turning away from Christ, the deliberate rejection of what they had experienced. For these readers, it would mean renouncing Christ and returning to Judaism to escape persecution. Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a solemn call to persevere.

To restore them again to repentance. Key words. “Restore” (anakainizein, renew). “Again”: they had shown repentance once. It is impossible to bring them back. Why? Because they have rejected the only means of repentance and forgiveness: Christ’s sacrifice. There is no other sacrifice (10:26). If you reject the only remedy, there is no remedy left.

Since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm. Key words. “Crucifying once again” (anastaurountas, crucifying again, or crucifying up). Present tense: they continue doing it. By rejecting Christ, they side with those who crucified him and declare that he deserved it. “To their own harm” (heautois, for themselves, to their loss).

And holding him up to contempt. Key words. “Holding up to contempt” (paradeigmatizontas, exposing to public shame, making a public example of). Publicly declaring that Christ is not worth following, they shame him before the world. The present tense explains the impossibility: as long as they continue in this attitude, repentance is impossible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that anyone worried about having committed this sin has committed it. Those who fear they have fallen away and long to return to Christ show that their hearts are not hardened. The hardened do not care. Nor does it limit God’s power absolutely; it describes the condition of the hardened apostate, whom God has given over to his choice.

In a sentence. and who then turn away, to be brought back to repentance, because they are nailing the Son of God to the cross all over again, to their own ruin, and holding him up to public scorn.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you have fallen away, that very fear is evidence of a tender heart. Come back to Christ now. He receives all who come (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a real warning against turning away from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.

For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it. Key words. “Drunk” (piousa, drunk in, absorbed). “Rain that often falls”: God’s repeated blessings, the gospel preached again and again, the Spirit’s work, the fellowship of believers (vv. 4–5). Both kinds of land receive the same rain.

And produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated. Key words. “Produces” (tiktousa, gives birth to). “Useful” (euthetos, fitting, suitable). Good land responds to the rain with fruit. Genuine believers bear fruit (Matthew 7:16–20; John 15:5, 8).

Receives a blessing from God. Key words. Fruitful land is blessed further.

But if it bears thorns and thistles. Key words. “Thorns and thistles” (akanthas kai tribolous): the curse of Genesis 3:17–18. Land that receives the same rain but produces only weeds shows its true nature.

It is worthless and near to being cursed. Key words. “Worthless” (adokimos, failing the test, rejected). “Near to being cursed” (kataras engys, close to a curse).

And its end is to be burned. Key words. Farmers burned fields of weeds. A picture of final judgement (10:27; Matthew 3:10, 12; John 15:6). The fruit shows the soil; the soil determines the end.

What it does not mean. The illustration does not mean the same land changes from good to bad. It shows that the same blessings fall on different kinds of ground, and the fruit reveals the difference. This supports the view that the apostates of verses 4–6 were never good soil.

In a sentence. Land that soaks up the rain that falls on it again and again and produces a crop useful to those who farm it receives God’s blessing. But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless and in danger of being cursed; in the end it will be burned.

On a Tuesday. What fruit is God’s rain producing in your life? Thank him for any growth, and ask him to pull up the thorns.

verseByVerse.quote: Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.

Though we speak in this way. Key words. The author recognises the severity of his warning.

Yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things. Key words. “Beloved” (agapētoi): the only time he uses this warm word. “Feel sure” (pepeismetha, have been persuaded, perfect tense: are confident). “Better things” (ta kreissona), the letter’s key word.

Things that belong to salvation. Key words. “Belong to” (echomena, hold onto, accompany, are connected with). There are things that accompany genuine salvation, which the apostates of verses 4–6 lacked, and which the readers show. This is the key to the passage: the experiences of verses 4–5 can happen without salvation; the fruit described in verse 10 accompanies it.

For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work. Key words. “Unjust” (adikos). God is faithful to his promises; he will not forget the fruit of faith. Not that the work earns salvation, but that it is evidence of it, which God will acknowledge (Matthew 10:42; 25:34–40).

And the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do. Key words. “Love” (agapēs). “For his name” (eis to onoma autou): for God’s sake. “Serving” (diakonēsantes, having served, and diakonountes, continuing to serve). They had cared for persecuted believers (10:32–34), and still did. Love for fellow believers is a mark of genuine faith (1 John 3:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works save or that God owes us salvation for them. It means God will justly acknowledge the fruit of faith, which is itself his gift (Ephesians 2:10). Nor does the author’s confidence make the warning unnecessary; the warning is one of the means by which they will persevere.

In a sentence. Even though we speak like this, dear friends, we are confident of better things in your case, the things that come with salvation. God is not unfair; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown for him by helping his people, as you still do.

For worship. Thank God that he sees and remembers every act of love you do for his people. None is forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness. Key words. “Desire” (epithymoumen, long for). “Each one” (hekaston): personal concern for every individual. “Earnestness” (spoudēn, diligence, zeal). The same zeal they showed in love, they should show in hope.

To have the full assurance of hope until the end. Key words. “Full assurance” (plērophorian, full conviction, certainty). “Of hope”: the hope of glory (3:6). “Until the end” (achri telous), as in 3:14. Assurance is possible and is to be pursued diligently. It is not presumption but a fruit of faith (10:22; 2 Peter 1:10).

So that you may not be sluggish. Key words. “Sluggish” (nōthroi), the same word as “dull” in 5:11. They had become sluggish in hearing; they must not become sluggish in hope.

But imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises. Key words. “Imitators” (mimētai). “Faith” (pisteōs) and “patience” (makrothymias, long-suffering, patient endurance). “Inherit the promises”: the faithful of the past, like Abraham (vv. 13–15) and the heroes of chapter 11, received what God promised through persevering faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean assurance comes by our own efforts. It comes from God’s promise (vv. 17–18), but we are to pursue it diligently, using the means God gives: Scripture, prayer, sacraments, fellowship, obedience.

In a sentence. We want each of you to show this same eagerness right to the end, so that you have full assurance of what you hope for. We do not want you to become lazy, but to follow the example of those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.

On a Tuesday. Who is a believer from the past or present whose faith and patience you could imitate? Read about them this week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Two Unchangeable Things, and an Anchor Behind the Curtain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God made his promise to Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater, and Abraham, after waiting patiently, received what was promised. People swear by something greater, and an oath settles a dispute. So God, wanting to show the heirs of the promise how unchangeable his purpose is, confirmed it with an oath. By these two unchangeable things, in which God cannot lie, we who have fled to him for refuge are strongly encouraged to hold fast to our hope. It is a sure anchor for the soul, entering behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of us.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Anchor That Goes Upward

God confirmed his promise with an oath so that we might have strong encouragement. Our hope is anchored behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as forerunner.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac, not always steadily, and obtained the promise.

Now: We are those who have fled for refuge. The storm and the anchorage are in different places.

verseByVerse.quote: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.

For when God made a promise to Abraham. Key words. Abraham is the great example of one who through faith and patience inherited the promises (v. 12). God promised him descendants, land and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–3; 15:5; 17:4–8).

Since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself. Key words. “Swore” (ōmosen). After Abraham was willing to sacrifice Isaac, God confirmed his promise with an oath, the only time in Genesis he swore to Abraham: “By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD” (Genesis 22:16). People swear by someone greater; there is no one greater than God, so he swore by himself.

Surely I will bless you and multiply you. Key words. From Genesis 22:17. “Surely” (ei mēn, certainly, a strong oath formula). The doubled Hebrew (“blessing I will bless you, multiplying I will multiply you”) underlines the certainty.

And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise. Key words. “Patiently waited” (makrothymēsas). Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac (Genesis 12:4; 21:5). “Obtained the promise” (epetychen tēs epangelias): he received Isaac, the first fulfilment, though the full inheritance was still future (11:13, 39–40).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham received everything promised in his lifetime. He saw the beginning; the fulfilment came in Christ and will be completed in the new creation (11:10, 16).

In a sentence. When God made his promise to Abraham, since there was no one greater for him to swear by, he swore by himself, saying, “I will certainly bless you and give you many descendants.” And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham received what was promised.

On a Tuesday. What promise of God are you waiting for? Wait patiently, like Abraham. God keeps his word.

verseByVerse.quote: For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.

For people swear by something greater than themselves. Key words. In human affairs, an oath calls on a higher authority as a witness and guarantor.

And in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. Key words. “Final” (peras, end, limit). “Confirmation” (bebaiōsin, guarantee, legal validation). An oath ends argument: it settles the matter.

So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise. Key words. “Heirs of the promise”: Abraham, and all who share his faith (Galatians 3:29). God did not need to swear, since his word is enough. But in kindness he stooped to our weakness and added an oath.

The unchangeable character of his purpose. Key words. “Unchangeable” (ametatheton, immovable, irrevocable, a legal term for a will that cannot be altered). “Purpose” (boulēs, counsel, plan, will). God’s saving plan cannot change (Romans 11:29; Ephesians 1:11).

He guaranteed it with an oath. Key words. “Guaranteed” (emesiteusen, mediated, stood as guarantor). God made himself the guarantor.

So that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie. Key words. The two things: God’s promise and God’s oath. Both are unchangeable, because God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2). “Impossible” (adynaton): the same word as verse 4. It is impossible for apostates to be renewed; it is equally impossible for God to break his word to his own.

We who have fled for refuge. Key words. “Fled for refuge” (hoi kataphygontes). An allusion to the cities of refuge in Israel, where a person who killed someone accidentally could flee for safety from the avenger (Numbers 35; Joshua 20). Believers have fled to God in Christ for safety from judgement.

Might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. Key words. “Strong encouragement” (ischyran paraklēsin, powerful comfort). “Hold fast” (kratēsai, seize, grasp firmly). “The hope set before us” (tēs prokeimenēs elpidos, the hope lying ahead): eternal salvation in God’s presence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God needs an oath to be trustworthy. He added it for our sake, to strengthen weak faith.

In a sentence. People swear by someone greater than themselves, and an oath confirms what is said and ends all argument. Because God wanted to make the unchangeable nature of his purpose very clear to the heirs of what was promised, he confirmed it with an oath. He did this so that, by two unchangeable things in which God cannot possibly lie, we who have fled to him for safety may be greatly encouraged to hold on to the hope set before us.

For worship. God has given you his word and his oath. Rest your full weight on them today. It is impossible for him to lie.

verseByVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.

We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul. Key words. “This”: the hope (v. 18). “Anchor” (ankyran). In the ancient world, the anchor was a symbol of hope and stability. Early Christians carved anchors in the catacombs. “Sure” (asphalē, secure, safe, not slipping). “Steadfast” (bebaian, firm, reliable). An anchor keeps a ship from drifting (2:1) in a storm. Our hope holds us steady.

A hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain. Key words. “Enters” (eiserchomenēn). The image shifts: our anchor is not sunk in the sea bed but fixed in heaven itself. “Inner place behind the curtain”: the Most Holy Place of the tabernacle, separated by a heavy curtain, where God’s presence dwelt (Exodus 26:31–33; Leviticus 16:2, 12). The high priest passed behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place only once a year. Our hope is anchored in God’s very presence, where nothing can move it.

Where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf. Key words. “Forerunner” (prodromos, one who runs ahead). The word was used of a scout sent ahead of an army, or of a small boat that carried a ship’s anchor ahead into the harbour when the water was too shallow for the ship to enter, fixing it to a rock so the ship could be pulled in. The Old Testament high priest went in alone and came out; no one followed. Jesus goes ahead so that we can follow him (10:19–20). “On our behalf” (hyper hēmōn): as our representative.

Having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Key words. The words of Psalm 110:4 again, bringing the author back to the subject he paused at in 5:10. Chapter 7 will now explain.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our hope depends on how strongly we feel. An anchor holds the ship, not the other way round. Our hope is secure because of where it is fixed: in Christ, in God’s presence.

In a sentence. This hope is an anchor for our souls, firm and secure. It reaches into the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus, who went ahead of us, has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest for ever, in the order of Melchizedek.

For worship. In whatever storm you face, remember: your anchor is fixed in heaven, in Christ. You will not drift away.
verseByVerse.note: The high priest passed behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year, on the Day of Atonement.

7.title: The Order of Melchizedek: A Priest Forever
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the theological centre of Hebrews. From two brief Old Testament references, Genesis 14:17–20 and Psalm 110:4, the writer argues for the supremacy and finality of Jesus’ priesthood over the whole Levitical system.

Melchizedek was king of righteousness and king of peace, priest of God Most High, king and priest in one. Genesis gives him no genealogy, birth or death, and that silence makes him a picture of the eternal Son. Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, so Melchizedek was greater than Abraham and, in Abraham, greater than Levi. If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, why promise another? Jesus is a priest “by the power of an indestructible life”, guarantor of a better covenant, able to save to the uttermost because he always lives to intercede.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Melchizedek, and What Abraham Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham after the battle, blessed him and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness; Salem means peace. Without recorded father, mother or genealogy, beginning or end, he resembles the Son of God and remains a priest. Abraham the patriarch paid him tithes and was blessed by him, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. Even Levi, still in Abraham’s body, paid tithes through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading the Silence of Scripture

Genesis gives Melchizedek no genealogy, and the writer reads the silence as a portrait of a priesthood that does not rest on descent. Abraham tithed to him and was blessed by him — the lesser by the greater.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid tithes to Melchizedek.

Now: Righteousness comes first, then peace; there is no peace with God that bypasses righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.

Meaning first. Hebrews 7 is the heart of the letter’s argument that Jesus is a better priest than the priests of Israel. It begins with Melchizedek, the mysterious priest-king who appears in Genesis 14 (vv. 1–3). His name and title mean king of righteousness and king of peace; Scripture records no genealogy, birth or death for him, so he stands as a picture of a priest who continues forever. He was greater than Abraham, because Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, and so greater than Levi, Abraham’s descendant, who in a sense paid tithes through Abraham (vv. 4–10). Then the argument: if perfection could have come through the Levitical priesthood, why would Psalm 110 speak of another priest in the order of Melchizedek? A change of priesthood means a change of law, and Jesus came from Judah, not Levi (vv. 11–14). He became priest not by physical descent but by the power of an indestructible life (vv. 15–17). The old commandment is set aside because it was weak and could not make anything perfect; a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God (vv. 18–19). Jesus was made priest with God’s oath, making him the guarantor of a better covenant (vv. 20–22). The old priests died and had to be replaced; Jesus lives forever, so he can save completely those who come to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them (vv. 23–25). He is exactly the high priest we need: holy, innocent, separate from sinners, exalted, who does not need to offer daily sacrifices, because he offered himself once for all (vv. 26–28).

For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God. Key words. Melchizedek appears in only three verses of Genesis (14:18–20) and one psalm (110:4). “King of Salem”: Salem was probably the early name of Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2). “Priest of the Most High God” (El Elyon): he worshipped the true God, the creator of heaven and earth, outside the line of Abraham. A priest and king in one person, as Christ is.

Met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him. Key words. Abraham had defeated four kings to rescue his nephew Lot (Genesis 14:1–17). Melchizedek brought out bread and wine and blessed him in the name of God Most High.

And to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. Key words. “A tenth” (dekatēn, tithe). Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils, recognising him as a priest of God.

He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness. Key words. The Hebrew name Malki-tsedeq means “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness.” Christ is the righteous King (Isaiah 9:7; 32:1; Jeremiah 23:5–6).

And then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace. Key words. “Salem” is related to shalom, peace. Christ is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who makes peace between God and sinners (Ephesians 2:14). The order matters: first righteousness, then peace. True peace comes only through righteousness (Psalm 85:10; Romans 5:1).

Where Christians differ: are believers required to tithe? Some teach that the tithe, a tenth of income, is binding on Christians, since Abraham tithed before the law of Moses. Verdict: Abraham’s tithe was a voluntary act of honour on a single occasion. The New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It teaches generous, regular, proportional, cheerful giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–15; 9:6–7). A tenth is a good starting guide for many, but Christians under grace should often give more, not less, and never under compulsion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Melchizedek’s name is merely a lucky coincidence. The author sees God’s providence shaping the Old Testament record to point to Christ.

In a sentence. This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham as he was returning from defeating the kings, and blessed him, and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means first “king of righteousness,” and then, since he was king of Salem, it also means “king of peace.”

For worship. Worship Christ as your King of righteousness and King of peace, who gives you peace with God through his righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.

He is without father or mother or genealogy. Key words. “Without father” (apatōr), “without mother” (amētōr), “without genealogy” (agenealogētos). Genesis records no parents, birth or death for Melchizedek. In Genesis, a book full of genealogies, this silence is striking. For a Levitical priest, genealogy was everything: a man could not serve unless he could prove descent from Aaron (Ezra 2:61–63). Melchizedek’s priesthood did not depend on descent.

Having neither beginning of days nor end of life. Key words. Scripture records neither. The author is arguing from the silence of the text: as Melchizedek appears in Scripture, he has no recorded beginning or end. He is a living picture of an eternal priesthood.

But resembling the Son of God. Key words. “Resembling” (aphōmoiōmenos, made like, made to resemble). Melchizedek is made like the Son, not the Son like Melchizedek. He is the copy; Christ is the original. The Son truly has no beginning or end; Melchizedek only appears that way in the record.

He continues a priest forever. Key words. “Continues” (menei, remains). “Forever” (eis to diēnekes, perpetually, continually). In the record, his priesthood never ends. In Christ, the reality.

Where Christians differ: was Melchizedek Christ himself? Some believe Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (a Christophany), or an angel. Verdict: Melchizedek was most likely a real, historical human king and priest, whose recorded life God arranged to foreshadow Christ. The text says he was “made like” the Son of God, which would be odd if he were the Son. He is a type, a living prophecy, not the reality itself. His lack of recorded genealogy is the point, not a claim that he literally had no parents.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Melchizedek was literally immortal or divine. It means the way Scripture presents him makes him a picture of Christ’s eternal priesthood.

In a sentence. No father, mother or family line is recorded for him, nor any beginning or end of his life; in this he is made to resemble the Son of God, and he remains a priest for ever.

For worship. Thank God that your High Priest truly has no end. He will never die, never be replaced, never stop praying for you.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis records no parents, birth or death for Melchizedek. The writer draws out the meaning of that silence, not a claim that Melchizedek had no parents.

verseByVerse.quote: See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.

See how great this man was. Key words. “See” (theōreite, consider, contemplate). “Great” (pēlikos, how great). The argument now shows Melchizedek’s superiority to Abraham, and therefore to Levi.

To whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! Key words. “Patriarch” (patriarchēs, founding father). Abraham was the most honoured figure in Israel’s history, the father of the nation. Yet he gave a tenth to Melchizedek. “Spoils” (akrothiniōn, the top of the heap, the best of the plunder).

And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people. Key words. Under the law of Moses, the Levites received tithes from the other tribes (Numbers 18:21–26).

That is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. Key words. The Levites took tithes from their own relatives, fellow descendants of Abraham, by a commandment of the law.

But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham. Key words. Melchizedek was not a Levite and had no legal right to tithes; he received them on the basis of his own greatness.

And blessed him who had the promises. Key words. Abraham was the bearer of God’s promises (Genesis 12:2–3), yet Melchizedek blessed him.

It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior. Key words. “Beyond dispute” (chōris pasēs antilogias, without any contradiction). In a formal blessing, the greater blesses the lesser (as a father blesses his children, Genesis 27; 48–49; or a priest blesses the people, Numbers 6:22–27). So Melchizedek was greater than Abraham.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that an ordinary believer cannot ask God to bless someone greater; this concerns formal, authoritative blessing.

In a sentence. Just think how great he was: even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the best of the plunder! The law requires the descendants of Levi who become priests to collect a tenth from the people, their own relatives, although they too are descended from Abraham. But this man, who did not trace his descent from Levi, collected a tenth from Abraham and blessed the one who had God’s promises. And without doubt the lesser person is blessed by the greater.

For worship. Bring your offerings to Christ, the greater Melchizedek, and receive his blessing. Every good gift comes through him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.

In the one case tithes are received by mortal men. Key words. “Mortal” (apothnēskontes, dying). The Levitical priests were dying men. One generation after another died and was replaced.

But in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. Key words. “Testified” (martyroumenos): Scripture witnesses. The record of Genesis says nothing of his death; and Psalm 110 says of the priest in his order, “You are a priest forever.” So in the record, he lives. And this points to Christ, who truly lives forever (v. 16).

One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham. Key words. “One might even say” (hōs epos eipein, so to speak). The author acknowledges this is a figurative way of speaking. Levi, the ancestor of the priests, was Abraham’s great-grandson.

For he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him. Key words. “Loins” (osphyi): the source of descendants. In Hebrew thought, an ancestor represents his descendants; what he does, they do in him (compare Romans 5:12, where all sinned in Adam). In a real sense, the whole Levitical priesthood bowed to Melchizedek when Abraham did. So Melchizedek’s priesthood is greater than Levi’s.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Levi was personally guilty or responsible for Abraham’s act. It is an argument from representation and headship, which the author marks as a manner of speaking.

In a sentence. In the case of the Levites, the tenth is received by men who die; but in Melchizedek’s case, by someone who, as Scripture testifies, is alive. You might even say that Levi, who collects the tenth, paid the tenth through Abraham, because when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in the body of his ancestor.

For worship. Thank God that you are represented before him not by dying men but by the living Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–28 — A Priest Forever, and the Change That Follows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, why promise another of a different order? A change of priesthood means a change of law. Jesus came from Judah, a tribe with no priests, and he is a priest not by descent but by the power of an indestructible life. The old command is set aside as weak; a better hope lets us draw near to God. God swore an oath to this priesthood, making Jesus guarantor of a better covenant. The old priests were many because they died; he lives forever, so he saves completely those who come to God through him, always interceding. Holy and exalted, he offered himself once for all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Change the Priesthood and the Law Must Follow

The law rested on the Levitical priesthood, and God has replaced that priesthood by oath with a priest who holds office by the power of an indestructible life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The former priests were many, because death stopped each one.

Now: He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.

Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood. Key words. “Perfection” (teleiōsis, completion, bringing to the goal): a keyword of Hebrews. Perfection here means bringing people fully into God’s presence, with sins dealt with completely and consciences cleansed (9:9; 10:1, 14). The Levitical priesthood could not do this.

For under it the people received the law. Key words. The law and the priesthood were bound together: the law established the priesthood, and the priesthood administered the law. They stand or fall together.

What further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek? Key words. The decisive argument: Psalm 110 was written by David, long after the Levitical priesthood was established. If the Levitical priesthood had been sufficient, why would God promise a new priest of a different order? The promise itself proves the old system was inadequate and temporary.

Rather than one named after the order of Aaron? Key words. The new priest is not in Aaron’s line.

For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well. Key words. “Change” (metatithemenēs, transfer, alteration). Since the law of Moses was tied to the Levitical priesthood, a new priesthood means the whole Mosaic covenant arrangement changes. This is radical: the old covenant system, with its sacrifices, priesthood and ceremonies, has been replaced.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s moral law has changed. The moral standards expressed in the Ten Commandments reflect God’s unchanging character and are confirmed in the New Testament (Romans 13:8–10). What changed is the ceremonial and priestly system, the covenant administration, which pointed forward to Christ.

In a sentence. If perfection could have been reached through the Levitical priesthood, on which the law given to the people was based, why was there still a need for another priest to come, one in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed too.

For worship. Thank God that you are not under a system that could never make you perfect, but under Christ, who has made you perfect forever (10:14).

verseByVerse.quote: For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.

For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe. Key words. “Another tribe” (phylēs heteras, a different tribe). Jesus was not from Levi.

From which no one has ever served at the altar. Key words. “Served” (proseschēken, attended to, officiated). Under the law, only Levites, and only Aaron’s descendants as priests, could serve at the altar. King Uzziah of Judah was struck with leprosy when he tried to burn incense (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah. Key words. “Evident” (prodēlon, clearly known, obvious). “Descended” (anatetalken, sprung up, risen like the sun or a sprouting plant). Jesus was of the tribe of Judah, the royal tribe of David (Matthew 1:1–16; Luke 3:23–33; Revelation 5:5). The Messiah was promised to come from Judah (Genesis 49:10).

And in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests. Key words. The law of Moses made no provision for priests from Judah. Under the law, Jesus could not have been a priest. His priesthood must be of a different order altogether.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus was unqualified. He was qualified by something far greater than tribal descent (v. 16). Nor does it mean the Levitical priesthood was wrong; it was God-given, but temporary.

In a sentence. The one these things are said about belonged to a different tribe, and no one from that tribe has ever served at the altar. For it is clear that our Lord came from the tribe of Judah, and Moses said nothing about priests coming from that tribe.

For worship. Praise Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who is both your King and your Priest.

verseByVerse.quote: This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”

This becomes even more evident. Key words. “Even more evident” (perissoteron eti katadēlon, much more obvious still). The change of law becomes even clearer.

When another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek. Key words. “Another” (heteros, of a different kind). “Likeness” (homoiotēta, resemblance), as in verse 3.

Who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent. Key words. “Legal requirement” (nomon entolēs, law of a commandment). “Bodily descent” (sarkinēs, fleshly, physical). The Levitical priesthood depended on physical ancestry: a merely external, earthly qualification.

But by the power of an indestructible life. Key words. “Power” (dynamin). “Indestructible” (akatalytou, that cannot be dissolved, destroyed, or broken down). Jesus’ qualification is his own resurrection life, which death could not destroy. He died, but death could not hold him (Acts 2:24); he rose to an endless life. His priesthood is based not on genealogy but on who he is and on his victory over death.

For it is witnessed of him, You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek. Key words. Psalm 110:4. The word “forever” is the key: only someone with an indestructible life could be a priest forever.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus did not truly die. He died truly and rose truly. His life is indestructible in that death could not keep him and he will never die again (Romans 6:9; Revelation 1:18).

In a sentence. And it becomes clearer still when another priest like Melchizedek appears, one who has become a priest not by a rule about human ancestry but by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed. For Scripture testifies about him: “You are a priest for ever, in the order of Melchizedek.”

For worship. Rejoice that your High Priest has an indestructible life. Death could not stop him, and nothing can stop his care for you.

verseByVerse.quote: For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.

For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside. Key words. “Set aside” (athetēsis, annulment, cancellation, a legal term for annulling a decree). The former commandment, the law establishing the Levitical priesthood, is cancelled.

Because of its weakness and uselessness. Key words. “Weakness” (asthenes, powerlessness). “Uselessness” (anōpheles, unprofitableness). Not that the law was bad, but that it was weak for this purpose: it could not achieve full cleansing and access to God. The weakness lay in the flesh it worked through (Romans 8:3).

For the law made nothing perfect. Key words. “Made perfect” (eteleiōsen). The law pointed to perfection but could not provide it (9:9; 10:1). It was a shadow (10:1), a tutor until Christ came (Galatians 3:24).

But on the other hand, a better hope is introduced. Key words. “Better hope” (kreittonos elpidos). “Introduced” (epeisagōgē, brought in besides, ushered in). The new covenant hope in Christ.

Through which we draw near to God. Key words. “Draw near” (engizomen, come close). The whole purpose of priesthood: access to God. Under the law, the people stayed at a distance; only the high priest drew near, once a year. Through Christ, every believer can draw near (4:16; 10:19–22; James 4:8). This is the better hope.

What it does not mean. “Uselessness” does not mean the law had no value. It was God’s gift, holy and good (Romans 7:12), and it served its purpose of pointing to Christ. But it could not do what only Christ could do.

In a sentence. The earlier regulation is cancelled because it was weak and could not achieve its goal (for the law brought nothing to perfection), and in its place a better hope is brought in, through which we come near to God.

For worship. Draw near to God today, not at a distance, but through Christ, with the better hope he has brought.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ‘You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.

And it was not without an oath. Key words. “Oath” (horkōmosias, oath-swearing). Another sign of superiority. God’s oath gives absolute certainty (6:16–18).

For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath. Key words. Aaron and his sons were appointed by command, not by oath (Exodus 28–29).

But this one was made a priest with an oath. Key words. Psalm 110:4 begins: “The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind.”

The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, You are a priest forever. Key words. “Change his mind” (metamelēthēsetai, regret, repent). God will never revoke this appointment. Christ’s priesthood is permanent and irrevocable.

This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant. Key words. “Guarantor” (engyos, surety, one who pledges himself, a legal term for someone who guarantees a debt or obligation with his own life or property). The word is used only here in the New Testament. Jesus personally guarantees that the new covenant will be fulfilled. He stands surety for his people: he pledges that their debts are paid and that God’s promises to them will be kept. “Better covenant” (kreittonos diathēkēs): the first mention of “covenant” in Hebrews; chapter 8 will develop it as the new covenant of Jeremiah 31.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God was uncertain about the old priesthood and certain only about the new. Rather, the old was always meant to be temporary; the new was meant to be permanent, and the oath marks that.

In a sentence. And this was not done without an oath. Others became priests without any oath, but he became a priest with an oath when God said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest for ever.’” Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he stands as your guarantor. Every promise of the new covenant is secured by his life.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.

The former priests were many in number. Key words. Josephus counted eighty-three high priests from Aaron to the destruction of the temple in AD 70. One after another.

Because they were prevented by death from continuing in office. Key words. “Prevented” (kōlyesthai, hindered). Death interrupted every priest’s ministry. Aaron died on Mount Hor, and his son Eleazar was dressed in his garments (Numbers 20:23–29). Every priest’s intercession ended at death.

But he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Key words. “Permanently” (aparabaton, unchangeable, non-transferable, that cannot pass to another). Christ’s priesthood will never pass to a successor. He has no successor, because he never dies.

Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost. Key words. “Able” (dynatai, has power). “To the uttermost” (eis to panteles, completely, fully, entirely, and for all time). Both senses are present: he saves completely (nothing left undone) and forever (no end to his saving work). There is no sinner too far gone, no sin too great, no time too long.

Those who draw near to God through him. Key words. “Draw near” (proserchomenous, those who come). Through Christ alone (John 14:6). This describes believers: those who keep coming to God through Christ.

Since he always lives to make intercession for them. Key words. “Always lives” (pantote zōn). “Make intercession” (entynchanein, plead, intervene, appeal on behalf of). Christ’s intercession is not begging an unwilling Father, but his presence before the Father as the one whose sacrifice has been accepted, continually presenting his finished work on behalf of his people and asking for all they need (Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1). His intercession guarantees their perseverance: he prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and he prays for all his own (John 17:9, 15, 20, 24).

What it does not mean. Christ’s intercession does not mean his sacrifice was incomplete. His intercession is based on his finished sacrifice. Nor does it mean he prays for those who do not come through him; he intercedes for “them,” those who draw near (John 17:9).

In a sentence. There were many of those earlier priests, because death prevented them from continuing in office; but because Jesus lives for ever, his priesthood is permanent and passes to no one else. That is why he is able to save completely and for ever those who come to God through him, because he is always alive to plead for them.

For worship. Right now, Jesus is interceding for you. Thank him, and come to God through him with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.

For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest. Key words. “Fitting” (eprepen, suitable, appropriate), as in 2:10. Jesus is exactly the high priest sinners need.

Holy. Key words. “Holy” (hosios, devout, pious, pure toward God).

Innocent. Key words. “Innocent” (akakos, without evil, guileless, harmless toward people).

Unstained. Key words. “Unstained” (amiantos, undefiled, pure). The high priest had to avoid ritual defilement (Leviticus 21:10–15); Jesus was free from all moral defilement.

Separated from sinners. Key words. “Separated” (kechōrismenos, perfect tense: set apart, and remaining so). Not that he avoided sinners (he ate with them, Luke 15:2), but that he was utterly different from them in character, and is now exalted beyond their reach to harm him.

And exalted above the heavens. Key words. “Exalted” (hypsēloteros, higher). Raised to the highest place (4:14; Ephesians 4:10).

He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily. Key words. “Daily” (kath’ hēmeran). Priests offered daily sacrifices (Exodus 29:38–42), and the high priest offered yearly on the Day of Atonement. The repetition proved their inadequacy (10:1–4, 11).

First for his own sins and then for those of the people. Key words. As in 5:3 and Leviticus 16:6, 15. Jesus had no sins of his own.

Since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. Key words. “Once for all” (ephapax): a single, unrepeatable, completely sufficient act (9:12, 26, 28; 10:10). A keyword of Hebrews. “Offered up himself”: the priest was also the sacrifice. No animal; himself. This is the first explicit statement in Hebrews that Christ’s sacrifice was his own self.

For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests. Key words. “Weakness” (astheneian): sinful, mortal men.

But the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever. Key words. “Came later”: Psalm 110 was written centuries after the law of Moses, so it supersedes it. “Son”: the eternal Son of God. “Made perfect” (teteleiōmenon, perfect tense: completed and remaining so), as in 2:10 and 5:9. Fully qualified, forever.

Where Christians differ: is Christ’s sacrifice re-presented in the Mass? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the Mass is the same sacrifice of Calvary made present again in an unbloody manner, offered for the living and the dead. Verdict: Hebrews insists that Christ offered himself “once for all,” and that unlike the old priests he has no need to offer repeatedly (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–18). Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin (10:18). The Lord’s Supper is a memorial and a means of grace, in which believers by faith feed spiritually on Christ, who is truly present by his Spirit, but it is not a re-offering of his sacrifice.

What it does not mean. “Separated from sinners” does not mean Jesus is distant from sinners who come to him. He is exalted, yet sympathises (4:15).

In a sentence. Such a high priest is exactly what we need: holy, without evil, pure, set apart from sinners and raised higher than the heavens. Unlike the other high priests, he does not need to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for the people’s. He did that once and for all when he offered himself. For the law appoints as high priests men who are weak; but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect for ever.

For worship. Worship Jesus, the holy and spotless High Priest, who offered himself once for all. Your sins are dealt with completely.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him,<sup>2</sup>and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.<sup>3</sup>He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.<sup>4</sup>See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils!<sup>5</sup>And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham.<sup>6</sup>But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises.<sup>7</sup>It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.<sup>8</sup>In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.<sup>9</sup>One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham,<sup>10</sup>for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.<sup>11</sup>Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than
